To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
angiographic LL of 0.3-0.6 mm after DES implantation is not associated with a lower incidence of future critical events.
angiographic late loss between 0.30 and 0.60 mm is not a protective factor against critical events after 5 years of follow-up.
late loss between 0.30-0.60 mm after drug eluting stent implantation does not predict long-term clinical outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between angiographically measured late loss (LL), a surrogate of neointimal hyperplasia, and long-term clinical outcomes following drug-eluting stenting (DES).
the relationship between angiography late loss and long-term clinical outcomes after drug-eluting-stent implantation.
the relationship between angiography late loss and long-term clinical outcomes after drug-eluting-stent (DES) placement.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

angiographic LL <0,3 mm and LL between 0,3 and 0,6 mm are associated with a favorable long-term clinical outcome, whereas angiographic LL >0,6 mm is associated with a worse long-term clinical outcome.
a post-DES angiographic LL of <0.3 or >0.6 is predictive of future critical events.
angiographic LL >0 or <0.6 mm after DES implantation is associated with increased rates of future critical events.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
angiographic LL is not a reliable predictor for long-term clinical outcome in patients undergoing DES implantation.
angiographic LL is not necessarily a good surrogate marker of long-term clinical outcome.
angiographic LL is not a good surrogate for future clinical outcomes. (Korean Circ J 2012;42:13-18)
The main takeaway from our work is that
long lesion length and chronic renal failure are the two most important independent predictors for long-term critical events in patients with DES implantation.
angiographic LL >0, regardless of the magnitude, may be a surrogate marker of long-term clinical outcome.
long lesion length, rather than angiographic LL, is a more reliable predictor of long-term clinical events.
